name: Earthjustice: biodiversity (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the counted good is forest carbon kept out of the air, which spares people everywhere (heat deaths).
summary: Earthjustice's species, public-lands and oceans work (our judgment: 30% of its programme spending, $41.2M in the year to June 2025). The one win of fiscal 2022-2025 we can put on the site's scale is the Tongass National Forest's roadless protection, restored in January 2023 on 9.37 million acres after tribes and groups represented by Earthjustice sued, counted for the forest carbon logging would have released; the species wins (gray wolves relisted, other Endangered Species Act protections, a marine monument kept closed to fishing) count nothing, since whether more wild animals alive is a gain is unknown. At the defaults it comes to about 0.0000007 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the site's other conservation models because the Forest Service expected the 2020 exemption to change overall logging little, so the restored protection spares only about a hundred hectares a year of 3.8 million, much of that timber is cut elsewhere instead, and the protection is again under threat. The biggest uncertainties are how much logging the 2020 exemption would have brought, the years counted and the discount rate; the branch is discounted for missing data.

Tongass National Forest roadless areas whose protection was restored (January 2023)

source.title: KTOO Public Media (25 January 2023), Biden administration restores Roadless Rule protections to Tongass National Forest
source.quote: restored roadless protections to 9.37 million acres of the Tongass National Forest

rows.explainer: In January 2023 the US Department of Agriculture repealed the 2020 exemption that had opened the Tongass's roadless areas to road-building and logging, after tribes and conservation groups represented by Earthjustice sued over it.

rows.label: Tongass roadless areas restored to protection
rows.explainer: The acres in hectares: the protected area the win covers. Each hectare counts the yearly logging it is spared (next rows).

rows.label: Hectares in an acre
rows.explainer: The unit conversion, the site's shared figure (an international acre is 0.4047 hectares; NIST Handbook 44).

rows.label: Share of the roadless old growth that would have been logged a year under the 2020 exemption
rows.explainer: The Forest Service's own analysis of the 2020 exemption expected overall harvest not to change much (CRS); recent Tongass timber sales were of the order of 15 to 20 million board feet a year, roughly 200 to 400 hectares at 20,000 to 30,000 board feet an acre. What the exemption changes is a part of that moving into roadless old growth, and somewhat more cutting. Our judgment, 0.003% of the roadless area a year (0.0005% to 0.015%): about 110 hectares a year (20 to 570).

source.title: Congressional Research Service (2020), R46505, Proposed Alaska Roadless Rule and the Tongass National Forest
source.quote: overall harvest levels are not expected to vary significantly under the exemption
source.note: CRS quotes the Forest Service's 2020 environmental impact statement for the exemption.

rows.label: CO₂ released by logging a hectare of Tongass old growth
rows.explainer: Southeast Alaska's coastal temperate rainforest holds about 210 to 220 tonnes of carbon a hectare in its trees alone (Leighty et al. 2006), more with roots, dead wood and soils; logging releases most of the living carbon over a few decades (slash, decay, short-lived products) while regrowth takes a century to recover it. Our judgment, 700 t CO₂ a hectare (400 to 1,100), the net release counted when the stand is cut.

rows.label: CO₂ a protected hectare is spared a year (logging avoided × carbon released)
rows.explainer: Each protected hectare's expected avoided emissions a year: the share logged a year × the CO₂ a logged hectare releases.

rows.label: Years the restored protection counts
rows.explainer: A campaign's win counts the shared years a won reform counts (docs/normalization.md 2.9; families/conservation.md).

rows.label: Years from the win until logging would have reached the roadless areas
rows.explainer: Timber sales in newly opened areas take years of planning, environmental review, road-building and sale before cutting starts: our judgment, 3 years (1 to 6), anchored on the Forest Service's usual lead from a project decision to a timber sale.

rows.label: Years of protection, discounted
rows.explainer: Every year of protection, and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number. Future generations are the next two rows.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future years of healthy life kept, discounted
rows.explainer: Every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take from people not yet born (the long-run world population × the share lost), discounted for ever at the shared rate. How much future generations count is your discount rate.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Trust in the chain as built (the protected area, the carbon per hectare, the logging it is spared): the missing-data step already discounts the judged outcome, so this asks only whether the figures are biased. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), as in the climate sister model.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Logging that wouldn't have been avoided anyway in the years counted: the Forest Service's 2021 pause on large old-growth sales (the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy) was a policy a later administration could and did reverse, so it holds back little in the counted years; some roadless stands would have stayed uncut for lack of buyers. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 100%).

rows.label: Share of the win due to advocacy and litigation at all
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for the part of a won climate policy that is the advocates' doing (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the restored Tongass protection was also an administration's own climate and tribal-consultation choice.

rows.label: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy and litigation behind the restored protection
rows.explainer: Earthjustice was lead counsel for the Southeast Alaska tribes and conservation groups (Organized Village of Kake and others) that sued over the 2020 exemption and pressed for its repeal, beside the Southeast Alaska Conservation Council, Audubon, the Natural Resources Defense Council and the tribes' own work. Our judgment, 35% (15% to 60%).

rows.label: Earthjustice's share of all resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Advocacy's share of the win × Earthjustice's share of the advocacy (Convention 2).

rows.label: Earthjustice's own spending as a share of its resources (with credit by share of resources)
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources on, the donated legal work and advertising space count as others' resources behind the same wins (templates.md Convention 2). Off (the default), 1.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Share of the protection that lasts: in 2025 the Department of Agriculture announced it would rescind the national Roadless Rule and filed the proposal in August 2026, which Earthjustice is contesting; the Tongass's protection lasts only as long as the rule or a court order. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: No other funder's money moves with Earthjustice's on this: 1 (0.9 to 1.1).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no hectare spared or tonne avoided is measured; the logging and carbon are judged. Taken in full.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Other biodiversity wins of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value

source.title: Earthjustice, Annual Report, fiscal year 2025
source.quote: Our litigation also stopped the Trump administration's attempt at opening more than 300 million acres

rows.explainer: Other wins of the period with countable carbon or health left out: offshore and onshore lease sales challenged where they don't already count in the climate model's other wins, public-land sales stripped from the 2025 budget bill, and the habitat protections that keep carbon in the ground. The species wins themselves (gray wolves relisted in 2022, other Endangered Species Act listings, the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument kept closed to commercial fishing) count nothing here, like the wild-animal branch, since their welfare effect is unknown. Our judgment, 20% of the modelled value (5% to 50%).

rows.label: Leakage: logging moved elsewhere, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Timber not cut in the Tongass is largely cut elsewhere: Wear and Murray (2004) find that most of the federal harvest given up in the Pacific Northwest was made up by harvest on other US and Canadian lands. Those stands hold less carbon than Tongass old growth, so the carbon leaks less than the timber. Our judgment, −50% (−80% to −25%).

source.title: Wear, D. N. & Murray, B. C. (2004), Federal timber restrictions, interregional spillovers, and the impact on US softwood markets, Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 47(2)
source.note: Most of the federal harvest cut in the Pacific Northwest under the spotted-owl restrictions was offset by more harvest on other lands in the US and Canada.

rows.label: Other wins and leakage, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: The other wins added and the leakage taken off (families/conservation.md: leakage is a negative share here).

rows.formula: tco2e_bridged * (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier) / ($uov_per_daly)
